extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of hydrostatics / natural philosophers / educated readers interested in experimental fluid mechanics
extracted.subtask_description: A didactic, experimental exposition of hydrostatic principles (pressure vs depth, transmission of pressure, and paradoxical consequences) illustrated by several laboratory setups and numerical examples. The text explains what to observe, how to arrange valves and vessels, and what conclusions to draw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pressure depends only on column height (depth)
rubrics_metrics.description: No Part of a Horizontal Plane does ever bear a greater Burden than the Weight of the Column of Altitude which has that part for its basis and the given perpendicular Height (i.e., pressure at a point depends only on the vertical height of fluid above it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly as the central law: regardless of the shape, breadth, or total quantity of fluid, equal perpendicular heights give equal pressure on equal area. Examples: multiple tubes of different size all at same fluid height press equally on the common base; explicit references to Sect. XXXVIIL and numerical illustrations (height, area, pounds per cubic foot).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hydrostatic paradox (same pressure despite different quantities)
rubrics_metrics.description: A vessel (or many tubes) containing very different quantities of water will exert the same pressure on a common base provided the vertical height of the water above the base is the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by three tubes opening into a common base: each single tube alone presses with the full weight corresponding to its column height, yet when all are open together the total pressure on the base is not the sum of their weights but equals the pressure due to the single common height. Experimental demonstration: shut/open cocks G, E, F and observe base pressure; thought-experiment with intuition failing until law is applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pressure transmitted equally in all directions (upwards and downwards)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fluid pressure at a given point acts equally in all directions: e.g., the pressure upwards at a point F can be inferred from the pressure downwards at another point G when connected by a path of fluid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrated by drawing a thread from G to F entirely through the same fluid when the orifice is under water; used to reason that the pressure upward and downward are equal when the connecting path lies wholly in the fluid. See examples referencing Sects. XLIII, LX, LXI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orifice position (under-water vs in-air) affects transmitted pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: If the mouth (orifice) of a tube is under the water, a connecting thread passes only through water and pressure relations hold; if the orifice is above the water in the air, the connecting line must pass through air and the previous short computation fails because pressures are no longer equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains an experimental anti-pattern: when the tube mouth L is in the air PQOR, the thread from G to F must pass through air before reaching F, so F and G will not be pressed with equal force even if they are at equal parts of the same horizontal plane. Use the example to show where naive application of the equal-pressure idea breaks down.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small volume at great height can exert large pressure (height matters over mass)
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrow long tube filled to a great height (even though it contains little weight) can produce as large or larger pressure on a base as a wide shallow vessel, because pressure depends on vertical height rather than total mass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by filling a 36-foot tube of small bore which contains one cubic foot (63 lb) of water: when combined with a large cistern the arrangement yields counterintuitive requirements for equilibrium (e.g., needing hundreds of thousands of pounds to balance certain configurations). Numerical computation steps (area × height × 63 lb/ft^3) are shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fluid pressure can act upwards and lift lids/covers
rubrics_metrics.description: Fluids exert upward pressure that can raise or bend lids and covers; the upward pressure on a horizontal cover equals the weight of the vertical column corresponding to that area and height.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Mariotte's experiment where a small tube of 1 inch breadth and 14–15 inches length, when filled, lifted the lid of a tub and bent it outwards; the text quantifies the upward force for the whole cover using the same height-based rule (leading to huge total upward force when multiplied over the cover area).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental design: use of valves/cocks to isolate columns
rubrics_metrics.description: To test hydrostatic laws one must be able to open and shut passages (cocks) between fluid regions so as to isolate columns and observe the effect (or lack of effect) on remote parts of the apparatus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes machines (e.g., MNQR with cocks at K and L, funnel TS and glass tube GH) where opening/shutting cocks and pouring oil or water into the funnel allows observation of whether pressure at another point changes. Use these operations to check invariance of pressure under certain manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental detail: prevent leakage and ensure connected fluid path
rubrics_metrics.description: Setups must be sealed/adapted so no fluid leaks and so that the path between points is entirely through the fluid whose pressure relations are being tested (e.g., adapt tube mouth to vial to prevent water running out when inverted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical note: put a curved glass tube in an ounce vial almost full of water, adapted to the mouth so no water can run out when inverted; cement glass into tin tubes with emplastrum diachylon; bind to a transverse piece of wood to prevent stirring. These precautions avoid confounding effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of suspended drops and small perturbations as indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Small drops hanging at an orifice and their response to tiny additions of fluid or changes in pressure are sensitive diagnostics of pressure changes in the connected system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a drop of oil hanging at GH falls off upon the addition of a small quantity of oil into the funnel, but later opening/shutting cocks did not cause the drop to fall—used to infer that pressure in tube NH was unchanged by operations at the funnel when cocks were manipulated appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atmospheric pressure explained by same depth-law (implications for barometer and life)
rubrics_metrics.description: The same hydrostatic law applied to air explains barometer readings and the necessity of the pressure law for life and habitations: the air column height determines pressure in rooms; if air behaved like piled solids the internal pressure would be negligible and life would be impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning includes comparison of mercury column heights (e.g., 28–31 inches) and conversion to equivalent water and air columns (numerical scaling, e.g., 14× mercury height, then ×1000 for air vs water). Consequences drawn: in a shallow chamber the internal air pressure would be vastly smaller absent the fluid-pressure law, causing creatures to die under rarefaction and preventing sound/fire/smell transmission. References to air-pump experiments and barometer observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast with solids: fluids equalize horizontal-plane pressure unlike heaps
rubrics_metrics.description: Solid granular piles (sand) produce very different pressures at different positions even on the same horizontal plane, whereas fluids produce equal pressure at equal depths across the same horizontal plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sand-bank thought experiment: two bodies at same horizontal plane but different positions bear different pressures under a sand heap; replace sand with liquid and pressure on both bodies is equal. Use this to rebut objections invoking gravity alone rather than fluid-law behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and unresolved mechanism: laws predict effects though mechanical explanation remains incomplete
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the laws of hydrostatics predict and experimentally confirm many 'wonders', mathematicians and mechanicians differ or are uncertain about the precise manner in which stagnant fluids produce these forces; mechanical analogies (e.g., special levers) have been proposed but do not fully explain the fluid phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Varignon, De la Hire, Mariotte and Whiston: one may invent lever analogies that reproduce effects in solids, but explaining why liquids at rest behave thus remains difficult. Use this as a caution about overconfident mechanistic claims even when empirical laws hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative practice: compute forces using area, height, and unit weight
rubrics_metrics.description: To compute the actual force/weight corresponding to fluid pressure, multiply base area by perpendicular height and by unit weight (e.g., 63 lb per cubic foot for water), then compare with balancing weights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple worked numerical examples: cistern 12 ft × 12 ft area × 8 in height → 96 cu ft → 6048 lb; tube 36 ft × small bore → 1 cu ft → 63 lb; larger vessel 12×12×36 → 5184 cu ft → 326592 lb. These calculations demonstrate paradoxical scales of force and how to set up balances to measure them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of balancing/loose-bottom apparatus to demonstrate equilibrium
rubrics_metrics.description: A loose wooden bottom lying on a cistern brim and attached by a string through the tube to a balance scale is an effective apparatus to show how fluid pressure at depth produces weight and equilibrium phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed setup: loose bottom WZ with ring at E, string through square tube tied to balance HGF; add known weight I on the balance and pour water into cistern and tube to observe whether bottom is raised. This illustrates that adding small weight may not be sufficient to raise the bottom when large effective pressures from remote columns exist.
